title: Shantanu and Ganga

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shantanu and Ganga: Vasishtha's cow, a curse he couldn't unsay, and why the eighth son had to live. Did you add a better word after one you couldn't take back? Day seven hundred eight.

The Ganga has gone shallow. Shantanu notices it while he's out hunting, following a wounded deer along the bank. The great river is barely moving, as if something upstream were holding it back. Ganga left him long ago, carrying their baby into the water, and he has ruled alone since then. Now he forgets the deer and goes looking for the reason instead, to find out what on earth could stop it.
screen: `THE RIVER HAS GONE SHALLOW.` → `THE KING LEAVES THE DEER.` → `WHAT COULD STOP A RIVER?`

segments.voice: By the water he finds a young man, tall and handsome, standing at the water's edge. He has stopped the Ganga's flow with arrows, a dam of them across the current. Shantanu has never seen anything like it. And he has no idea who this is. The young man sees the king, and with a power of illusion he clouds the king's senses and vanishes. So Shantanu is left on the bank with a suspicion. Could that have been my son? He calls on Ganga: show me the child. And she rises from the river in a beautiful form, holding the young man by the hand. This, she tells him, is your eighth son, the one I took with me. The text knows him by two names: Devavrata, and Gangeya, Ganga's son. Now look at the order the scene is told in. Shantanu sees what this young man can do before he knows who he is. He watches a stranger hold back a river. He loses him. And then he has to be introduced to his own child by the boy's mother. The son grew up out of his father's sight. When they finally meet, the father has to start where anyone would, with a name and a question. Some readers hear in the dam of arrows a first look at the strength this son will carry through the whole long poem. For now, a king who lost eight sons is standing beside one of them.
screen: `A DAM OF ARROWS.` · `THE STRANGER VANISHES.` · `SHOW ME THE CHILD.` · `DEVAVRATA, GANGA'S SON.` · then, large: `INTRODUCED TO HIS OWN SON.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest and your breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone close who has changed while you weren't watching: a child who grew up, a parent who grew older, a friend you lost touch with. Breathe in, and see them as they were when you last really looked. Breathe out, and let that picture loosen. Leave a little room for who they are now, someone you might need to meet again. Stay with them for a few more breaths. The bell holds the time.
Shantanu and Ganga. A river held back by arrows, and a father meeting the son the river raised.
Your line: Shantanu and Ganga. Today, ask someone close a question you'd usually save for a stranger. Day seven hundred eight.

howItsDone: In some Hindu families a child is formally named in a ceremony called namakarana, where the name is spoken aloud and the child is introduced to family and elders.

original.note: Sanskrit Devavrata, a name of Shantanu and Ganga's eighth son; the text also calls him Gangeya.

trapdoor: what you thought: a father and son run into each other by a river.
what it means: the father sees his son's strength first, and has to be introduced to him.
what a scholar hears: the dam of arrows on the shallow Ganga, and the son's two names, Devavrata and Gangeya.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Shantanu finds the Ganga shallow; the youth and the arrows; Ganga presents their son)

notes: Check: Shantanu following a wounded deer along the Ganga; the river shallow; the youth checking the current with arrows; the youth confounding the king's senses by illusion and vanishing; Shantanu asking Ganga to show the child; Ganga appearing adorned, holding him by the right hand.
The names Devavrata and Gangeya are given in Ganguli where Ganga departs with the child; the script places them at this meeting. Confirm the placement.
'Ganga left him long ago' avoids the number of years; confirm Ganguli does not make the gap central.
'Some readers hear in the dam of arrows' is an unattributed interpretation; a Keeper may cut it.
howItsDone describes namakarana in general terms; confirm.

Editor (y3 audit): 'the text gives him two names here' became 'the text knows him by two names' (Ganguli names him where Ganga departs, not at this meeting); 'beautifully adorned' became 'in a beautiful form' (Ganguli adorns the boy); cut 'the river runs again', which the passage does not say.

Audit (y3, 707-716): 'follows the river upstream' and 'Upstream he finds' became 'goes looking for the reason' and 'By the water' (Ganguli has the king wonder at the shallow river, then see the youth; no upstream walk).
